analysis.one_liner: Bars former members of Congress and top officials from lobbying for foreign governments.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 3 cosponsors from both parties, never received a committee vote or House floor action before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Foreign Agents Registration Act to permanently prohibit anyone who has served as a member of Congress, a senior presidential appointee, or a general or flag officer in the military from registering as, or serving as, an agent of a foreign principal — in plain terms, from lobbying for foreign governments or foreign political interests. It would also extend the existing one-year 'cooling off' restriction on representing foreign entities to cover these officials for life. The ban would apply only to officials whose service ended after the bill's enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, who would no longer see the former lawmakers and officials they know from public service cashing in by lobbying for foreign governments. It would also serve the national interest by reducing foreign governments' access to well-connected former U.S. officials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans concerned about foreign influence

how_it_helps.text: Would permanently bar anyone who served as a member of Congress, a senior political appointee, or a general or flag officer from registering under or serving as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act [S2][S3].

Would amend the post-employment restriction in federal law (18 U.S.C. 207(f)(1)) so that these officials could not represent foreign entities even beyond the existing one-year ban, making the restriction lifelong [S3].
Would apply only going forward, to officials whose congressional or military service ended on or after enactment, so it would not upend existing lobbying arrangements retroactively [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, senior executive appointees, and retired generals and admirals would lose a lucrative career path; foreign governments and foreign-aligned interests would lose access to well-connected former officials.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ex-lawmakers, ex-officials, and foreign lobbying firms

drawbacks.text: The bill's restriction is effectively permanent, which is more sweeping than the one-year cooling-off periods in current revolving-door law; critics of long lobbying bans argue they deter qualified people from government service and can be challenged as restricting political speech and the right to petition government.

The definitions cover a broad swath of senior executive branch personnel (presidential appointees, noncareer Senior Executive Service members, and schedule C appointees), so some would face the lifetime foreign-agent ban for comparatively junior or short appointments [S3].
The bill targets foreign principals only; it would do nothing about former officials lobbying for domestic interests, the larger share of the revolving-door economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: foreign governments would lose a direct line to former U.S. lawmakers and top officials, and the public would see less of the phenomenon of retired officials selling access to foreign capitals. The main costs fall on the individuals restricted, plus some deterrence of talented people entering government service. The bill is narrowly drawn — it does not touch domestic lobbying — so its practical impact would be modest but targeted at a well-recognized problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Gallagher (R-WI) introduced the bill on March 5, 2019, with a total of 3 cosponsors (1 Democrat and 2 Republicans) [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
In April 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it sat with no further action [S5].
No vote was ever taken in the House or Senate, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress, senior executive officials, and retired generals and admirals keep the option of lobbying for foreign governments, and foreign principals keep access to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ex-officials and the foreign lobbying trade

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican and cosponsored by members of both parties (1 Democrat, 2 Republicans), but with only 4 total supporters in the House it never reached the stage where a party split could be measured.

industries.industry: Foreign lobbying agents and firms (FARA registrants)
industries.note: The bill would cut off a profitable line of business — former members of Congress, senior appointees, and retired generals and admirals working as agents of foreign principals. Public benefit and industry cost run in the same direction here.

industries.industry: Foreign governments and foreign political interests
industries.note: They would lose direct paid access to former U.S. lawmakers and top military and executive officials. Their gain in influence is the public's loss.

industries.industry: Retired military flag officers and former senior officials
industries.note: They would lose a lucrative post-service career path, though the restriction applies only to service ending after enactment. Their loss of income is the flip side of reduced foreign influence-buying.
